summary: Implementation-bug scan of the FIXED batchMint. The minter-pinning fix is sound and closes the original drain vector. The nudge guard, totalPaid/dust accounting, and forceApprove max/0 pattern are all correct. The one substantive remaining issue is a cross-contract reentrancy via the ERC1155 onERC1155Received callback fired DURING the mint loop, which is gated by attacker control of the trusted minter and a pre-existing balance; verdict is conditional/low-to-medium. All other checked items are non-issues and are documented as such.

findings.description: batchMint has no nonReentrant guard. Inside the loop, nftMinter.mint(dispatcherIndex, recipient) mints an ERC1155 to a caller-controlled recipient; if recipient is a contract, the standard onERC1155Received hook fires DURING the loop. At that moment paymentToken approval to the minter is type(uint256).max (set line 205, revoked only at 211) and the nudge has not yet paid out. A reentrant call to batchMint is therefore possible mid-loop.
findings.attackVector: recipient is an attacker contract. During mint() the ERC1155 receiver hook re-enters batchMint. Two extraction angles were examined: (1) double-nudge: each batchMint reads the LIVE nudgePaymentToken balance (line 220) and sends the full balance; a re-entrant call that also clears count>=nudgeSize would read a now-zero balance after the outer/inner transfer, so the nudge cannot be paid twice from a single funding (balanceOf is re-read, not cached) -- NOT exploitable for double payout. (2) max-approval abuse: the outstanding max approval is to the minter (address(nftMinter)), a trusted owner-set contract, not to the attacker. The attacker cannot spend that approval directly; only the trusted minter can, and it only pulls the per-mint price. So the live approval is not directly drainable by the reentrant caller.
findings.reasoning: The reentrancy is real (no guard, contract recipient, callback mid-loop), but neither examined extraction path yields attacker profit: the nudge balance is re-read live (no stale double-pay), and the max approval is held by the TRUSTED minter, not the attacker. Reentry would simply pull payment from msg.sender for additional real, paid mints -- i.e. the attacker spends their own funds. The honest concern is bookkeeping confusion if the outer call's `remaining` (line 228) is computed after an inner call already swept the balance, but that only over- or under-refunds the caller's own funds within a single sender's nested calls (no cross-user theft). Recommend adding OZ ReentrancyGuard (already an expected dependency per the project CLAUDE.md) as defense-in-depth and to make the totalPaid accounting robust against nested re-entry. Severity LOW: no demonstrated cross-party value extraction; root cause is a missing guard rather than an exploitable invariant break.

findings.description: The dust/refund sweep reads paymentToken.balanceOf(address(this)) (line 228) as 'remaining' and computes totalPaid = paymentAmount - remaining. If a nested re-entrant batchMint (CODE-001, via the ERC1155 callback) for the SAME paymentToken runs to completion inside the outer loop, it performs its own pull and its own balance-based sweep. The outer call's `remaining` then reflects post-inner-sweep state, so the returned totalPaid can be skewed.
findings.attackVector: Same-token nested batchMint causes the balance-of accounting to conflate budgets of the two (possibly different) callers. Because the sweep sends the FULL contract balance to the outer msg.sender, an inner caller's unswept surplus could be paid to the outer caller, or vice-versa, depending on ordering. This is cross-caller fund misattribution under reentry, but requires an attacker to deliberately nest and only moves funds that were voluntarily supplied by the involved callers in the same tx; it does not touch the nudge pot or third-party funds.
findings.exploitability: requires self-induced reentry; bounded to participating callers' own deposits
findings.reasoning: Balance-snapshot accounting (balanceOf for `remaining`) is only safe if no nested call mutates the balance between snapshots. The mint-loop callback breaks that assumption. The practical impact is limited (a sender who reenters can over-refund themselves the contract's full balance, but that balance is sub-threshold dust plus their own current deposit), and a ReentrancyGuard (CODE-001 fix) fully eliminates it. Flagged separately because the root cause is the balance-of refund pattern, not just the missing guard. Severity LOW.

findings.description: count is caller-controlled with no upper bound; the loop runs count times. A large count exhausts the block gas limit.
findings.attackVector: Caller passes an enormous count. The transaction runs out of gas and reverts atomically.
findings.reasoning: The loop bound is the caller's own count and the only consequence of an over-large value is that the caller's own transaction reverts (out-of-gas) and rolls back, including the upfront pull. There is no shared queue, no per-block accumulator, and no other user's funds or liveness depend on this call. This is self-DoS, not protocol-DoS. Standard helper-looper pattern; QA at most. NOT a Medium.

findings.description: Nudge guard correctness verified (item 1) -- NO BUG. _nudgeTokenEntry is read once (199). The up-front guard (200) reverts only when the nudge token is set AND equals paymentToken; if nudgePaymentToken==0 the guard is correctly skipped. The payout block (215-226) re-checks _nudgeSize!=0 && count>=_nudgeSize and _nudgeTokenEntry!=address(0). Combinations: (a) nudgeSize==0 -> no payout regardless of token, correct (feature disabled); (b) nudgePaymentToken==0 -> guard skipped, payout inner-skipped, correct; (c) both set & token!=paymentToken -> payout of live balance, correct; (d) token==paymentToken & nudgeSize>0 -> reverts up-front before any pull, correct. There is NO path where the nudge pays while nudgePaymentToken==paymentToken (the up-front guard fires before the pull, and _nudgeTokenEntry is the same value reused). The dev's reuse of _nudgeTokenEntry (line 213 comment) is sound: the cached value is identical to a re-read because nudgePaymentToken cannot change between line 199 and line 219 within a single non-reentrant frame (and even under reentry a setter is onlyOwner). Stale/zero misuse: none -- a zero entry is explicitly inner-guarded at 219.
findings.reasoning: Up-front guard reverting even when nudgeSize==0 (nudge effectively disabled): observed and intentional. When nudgeSize==0 but nudgePaymentToken==paymentToken, the call reverts at 200 even though no nudge would pay. This is a slightly over-broad revert (a harmless config could be rejected) but is NOT a security bug -- it is fail-closed and the NatSpec (lines 36-38) documents 'whenever the nudge is configured'. Worst case is a usability nit where an owner who set nudgePaymentToken but nudgeSize==0 blocks batchMint for that paymentToken. Recommend (optional) gating the up-front guard on nudgeSize!=0 to match the payout condition, but this is QA/informational, not exploitable.

findings.description: totalPaid / dust accounting verified (item 4) in the non-reentrant case -- NO BUG. `remaining / DUST_THRESHOLD != 0` is an integer-division gate equivalent to `remaining >= DUST_THRESHOLD`, refunding only when surplus is at least 1e6 wei and leaving sub-threshold dust for the next batch (matches NatSpec 40-45). The `paymentAmount > remaining ? paymentAmount - remaining : 0` guard prevents underflow when a donation inflates the contract balance above paymentAmount (totalPaid clamps to 0). Donation skew: a pre-deposited donation simply gets swept to the current msg.sender (documented as 'donates to the next caller', 44-45) -- intended, not a refund-to-wrong-party bug in the single-call path. The refund always goes to msg.sender (line 230), never to recipient.
findings.reasoning: All arithmetic is correct and underflow-guarded in the normal (non-reentrant) execution path. The only way the balance-of snapshot misbehaves is under the reentry in CODE-002, which is filed separately. The donation-to-next-caller behaviour is explicitly documented and accepted.

findings.description: forceApprove max/0 pattern verified (item 5) -- NO BUG. forceApprove(max) at 205 then forceApprove(0) at 211 brackets the loop. If any inner mint reverts, the WHOLE tx reverts and the approval state (including the max approval) is rolled back atomically -- no residual approval persists across the failed tx. On success the approval is explicitly zeroed at 211. The approval is granted to the trusted owner-set minter only, never to a caller-controlled address. Even under the CODE-001 reentry, the dangling max approval is held by the trusted minter, which only pulls per-mint price; an attacker recipient is not the approved spender and cannot drain it.
findings.reasoning: Residual-approval risk on revert is eliminated by EVM atomic rollback. Residual approval on the happy path is eliminated by the explicit 0 at line 211. The only window where a non-zero approval exists is between 205 and 211, and it is scoped to the trusted minter. No issue.

findings.description: Access control & setters verified (item 6) -- NO SECURITY BUG. setTokenMinter/setNudgeSize/setNudgePaymentToken are onlyOwner with correct event emission (state-then-event, except setPauser which emits-then-sets to log the previous value -- a deliberate and correct ordering for a previous/new event). rescueERC20 is onlyOwner with a zero-recipient guard (151). The original drain vector (caller-supplied minter) is closed: the minter is pinned to owner state (194) and an unset minter reverts (195-197). Missing zero-checks: setTokenMinter(0), setNudgeSize(0), setNudgePaymentToken(0), setPauser(0) all intentionally DISABLE their respective features (documented), so absence of zero-checks is by design, not a bug.
findings.reasoning: No missing access modifiers, no event/state ordering bug that affects security (setPauser's emit-before-write is the canonical previous/new pattern). Zero-address 'disables' semantics are documented and intentional. rescueERC20 is owner-trusted and explicitly justified in NatSpec (142-149). Centralization (owner can rescue/redirect the nudge pot) is an accepted, documented trust assumption, not a finding.
